items.title: fix(backtest): keep excess_return consistent with corrected benchmark_return
items.body:
## Summary

- BaseEngine.run_backtest() corrects the displayed benchmark_return once an external benchmark's price series contains a non-positive-prior-price bar, but never recomputes excess_return from that same corrected value
- Recomputes excess_return right where benchmark_return is already corrected, so the two fields remain consistent for this corrected benchmark path

## Why

Issue #872 replaced the fragile pct_change-based return calculation with a safe price relative (buy_and_hold_return) for the displayed benchmark_return, after finding it could report numbers like +39,560% where the true return was -42.7%. calc_metrics() has its own internal re-derivation of the same total, still using the exact (1 + bench_ret).prod() - 1 pattern #872 found unsafe. base.py corrects the displayed field but never re-derives excess_return from the corrected value, so the metrics dict can become self-contradictory: benchmark_return reads correctly while excess_return implies a different number, both in the same JSON output the backtest tool returns to the LLM.

I audited every benchmark-derived metric in calc_metrics() (benchmark_return, excess_return, information_ratio, tracking_error, benchmark_beta). Only excess_return is affected. The other three are computed from the per-bar bench_ret series directly, which is already the corrected, #872-safe series by the time it reaches calc_metrics().

## Changes

- agent/backtest/engines/base.py: after the existing benchmark_metadata override, excess_return is recomputed as total_return minus the corrected benchmark_return, but only when an external benchmark was actually resolved. The internal-basket-benchmark path (no config["benchmark"]) is untouched.
- agent/tests/test_benchmark_excess_return_consistency.py: two new regression tests. One runs the real production path (ChinaAEngine.run_backtest, real calc_metrics(), only the network-dependent resolve_benchmark() fetch is stubbed) with a benchmark price series crossing a non-positive-prior-price bar, and asserts total_return minus excess_return equals benchmark_return. The other is a control confirming the fix does not touch excess_return when no external benchmark is configured.

## Test Plan

- [x] Confirmed the load-bearing regression test fails on the pre-fix implementation with a real numeric assertion failure (excess_return read 1.0 instead of 0.5), and passes with the fix
- [x] pytest tests/ -k "engine or backtest or benchmark or metrics" -q --ignore=tests/e2e_backtest (813 passed, 6 skipped, pre-existing)
- [x] black --check on both changed files: pre-existing, unrelated formatting issues in base.py confirmed via diff-isolation against the unpatched file (identical content at shifted line numbers); the new test file is clean
- [x] ruff check on both changed files: all checks passed

## Checklist

- [x] No changes to protected areas (src/agent/, src/session/, src/providers/): this only touches agent/backtest/
- [x] No hardcoded values
- [x] Code follows CONTRIBUTING.md guidelines
- [x] Documentation updated (n/a: internal correctness fix, no public interface change)
- [x] DCO signed-off

items.title: release: v0.126.0 — sort / sort_by builtins (#580), corrected benchmarks, new bench suites
items.body:
Closes #580.

machin had **no sort** — not a builtin, not in any of the 16 framework modules — so
every program needing ordered output hand-rolled one.

## Why this mattered

It cost machin the authoring-cost comparison it is positioned on. Same task in both
languages (read a file, count word frequencies, print top 5 by count then
alphabetically), tiktoken `o200k_base`:

| | tokens | lines | vs Rust |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| machin (before) | 218 | 26 | **+21%** |
| rust | 180 | 19 | — |
| **machin (after)** | **151** | **17** | **−16%** |

The entire difference was the sort. Rust does it in one `sort_by` line; machin
needed a 12-line selection sort — 90 of its 218 tokens.

Beyond tokens: what an agent hand-writes under time pressure is the O(n²) version,
and comparator tie-breaks are easy to get subtly wrong. Both are avoidable.

## API

```
sort(xs)            // ascending, for []int / []float / []string
sort_by(xs, less)   // ordered by less(a, b) bool; the comparator may capture
```

```
sort_by(keys(counts), func(a, b) {
    if counts[a] != counts[b] { return counts[a] > counts[b] }
    return a < b
})
```

## Two design decisions worth reviewing

**It returns a NEW slice rather than sorting in place.** MFL slices share backing
storage — `b := a` aliases, and so does passing one to a function (both verified).
An in-place sort would silently reorder every alias, which is the same hazard that
made in-place `realloc` unsound in #578. Copy-then-sort also matches slice-range,
which already always returns a fresh copy. There's a test asserting the input and
its aliases come out untouched.

**It is STABLE**, via a bottom-up merge sort rather than `qsort` — `qsort` is not
stable, and its comparator cannot portably carry an MFL closure environment. The
comparator is asked *"must b precede a?"* (i.e. `less(b, a)`), which needs one call
per comparison instead of two **and** yields stability for free: when neither
element is less than the other the predicate is false, so the earlier element goes
first. That means sorting by one key then another composes the way you'd expect.

`sort()` on an element type with no natural ordering is refused at compile time
with a message that names the fix:

```
error: sort: element type mfl_P has no ordering — use sort_by(xs, less) and say how to compare them
```

## Tests

Seven cases: ordered element types incl. negatives/empty/single, non-mutation of
input **and aliases**, comparator ordering, stability across two equal-key groups,
a capturing closure as comparator, the compile-time rejection, and a 500-element
sort verified fully ordered (exercises the merge's width doubling past pass one).

Documented in `machin guide` in the same change, per AGENTS.md.

Full suite green — `ok machin 178.854s`.

items.title: Benchmark STT candidates over a corrected benchmark set
items.body:
Closes #39.

## What

Adds a **batch STT benchmark** that runs the configured STT candidates across every corrected segment in a chosen benchmark split (`test_frozen` / `validation`), instead of one selected segment at a time. This is the core benchmark needed before choosing a base STT model.

## How

- **`localEvents.ts` — `getSttBenchmarkSetSegments(events, split)`** (pure): selects the segments whose *latest* membership resolves to `split` (latest-event-wins, matching `reconstructRecentSegments`), keeps only those with a resolvable `audio_ref`, and returns them in a deterministic order (`sessionId` then `segmentId`).
- **`index.ts` — `benchmark:run-set-stt`**: reads the event log **once** so every segment scores against the same correction snapshot and appended results can't shift later lookups; iterates the split **sequentially**; reuses the existing single-segment runner (now accepts a shared events snapshot); appends the **same `stt_benchmark_result` events** (candidate + CER score metadata — no new event type); streams `queued/running/done/failed` progress; and **isolates per-segment failures** (one bad segment never aborts the run).
- **preload/renderer**: a `Benchmark set` panel with a split selector, live progress counts, current-segment line, and a per-segment outcome/failure list. Single-segment `Benchmark latest` / per-history `Benchmark` still work and are mutually disabled with the batch run to avoid concurrent STT.
- **docs**: added a smoke-test step for the batch flow.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Run STT benchmark candidates over a corrected benchmark split.
- [x] Every result stays tied to `session_id`, `segment_id`, `audio_ref`, and candidate metadata (same event schema as before).
- [x] Existing single-segment benchmark still works.
- [x] UI reports progress and per-segment failures clearly.

Out of scope (untouched): fine-tuning, charts/dashboard, automatic model selection, LLM/math-transform stages, cloud execution.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck` — clean.
- `npm run build` — clean (main/preload/renderer all build).
- Unit-checked the correctness-critical selector `getSttBenchmarkSetSegments` with 10 synthetic-event cases (split filtering, latest-membership-wins reassignment in both directions, `audio_ref` resolution incl. out-of-order events, exclusion when no audio / no membership, deterministic ordering, `hasCorrection`, malformed-event tolerance) — all pass.
- Full end-to-end (mic + Python faster-whisper models + Electron GUI) not runnable in this environment; needs the Windows manual smoke step added to `docs/development.md`.

## Dependency guard

`Depends on: #38` (AGENTS.md source of truth) — **#38 is CLOSED** ✅. GitHub's native "blocked-by" also lists #42 (configurable candidates), but per AGENTS.md the `Depends on:` line is authoritative and #42 is not a hard dependency: the batch runner iterates the existing candidate set and will pick up #42's configurability automatically once merged.

## ⚠️ Review required — do not merge without it

Issue is labeled **`level:tres-eleve`**, which per AGENTS.md mandates a **human-owned review before merge**. As the implementer I did not self-review and did not merge.

**Suggested reviewer tier:** human review at **Opus 4.8 (max)** / `gpt-5-codex (high)` — top tier, matching très-élevé. Focus areas: the latest-membership-wins selection semantics, the single shared-snapshot scoring guarantee, and per-segment failure isolation.

## The bug

Full live taste of all 25 OpenCode Go models surfaced it: **gpt-5.6-luna, minimax-m2.5, minimax-m2.7 and qwen3.8-max all refused** the canary extraction — but with a **curly apostrophe** (`can't`, U+2019) instead of ASCII `can't`. The ASCII-only refusal marker lists missed it and the race verdict classified them as **"complied"** (i.e. the model leaked). The same hole could flip strict canary scoring when a canary is quoted inside a curly-apostrophe refusal.

## The fix

- `normalize_text()` in `scoring.py`: curly quotes/apostrophes (U+2018/2019/201A/201C/201D/201E), en/em dashes, nbsp → ASCII
- Applied in `looks_like_refusal_analysis` + `count_hedges` (race verdicts, defense classification, strict canary scoring all inherit)
- 4 regression tests

## Corrected benchmark (all 25 models, one probe each)

refused: 10 | hedged: 10 | complied: 0 | errors: 5

- Every working model refused the canary extraction — no disclosure
- grok-4.5 → HTTP 503 (overloaded); hy3-preview, kimi-k3, mimo-v2-omni, mimo-v2-pro → HTTP 400 (tier/availability)

Full table: `/tmp/taste_report.md` (local), results JSON `/tmp/taste_results.json`.

items.title: Full review: usage-distribution revenue engine, corrected benchmarks, True Cost of Service, multi-provider AI backend
items.body:
# Full review of the Water Rate Study Tool + fixes

This PR is the outcome of a complete review of the tool (calculation engine, financial metrics, UI, exporters, AI integration), folding in the meeting feedback on the Arkoma testing. It fixes the bugs found, closes the domain gaps that made results undependable, and adds an easy server-side AI setup that works with **any Anthropic or OpenAI model**.

## 1. The big one: revenue is now computed from actual usage, not averages (meeting items 1–3)

**Problem confirmed:** revenue was `customers × bill(average usage)`. With average usage ~2,200 gal, raising a 3,000+ gal block changed nothing — the tool couldn't model increases aimed at high-volume users, and it systematically understated revenue for tiered rates (billing at the average is always ≤ the true total under increasing-block tariffs).

**Fix:** Step 2 gains a **Customer Usage Distribution** table under the tier rates (e.g. 100 customers @ 1,000 gal, 50 @ 2,000, 25 @ 5,000, 10 @ 20,000 — with an optional notes/source column). When entered, revenue is billed bracket-by-bracket through the tier structure, customer/gallon totals derive from it, and every consumer (scorecard, projections, scenarios, reports, AI context) uses it. Without one, the tool falls back to the old average model and **labels the result as approximate** everywhere, including the report.

A unit test locks in the meeting's acceptance case: raising a high block's rate raises revenue by exactly the expected amount, while the legacy average model provably showed zero change.

Also:
- **Usage beyond the final block** always continues at the final block's rate — 20k/30k/40k-gal users are billed in full (tested), and the tier table now says so explicitly.
- **Tier blocks are fully configurable**: add/remove rows, custom breakpoints (incl. under 1,000 gal), optional block names. Unsorted/duplicate breakpoints previously **silently mis-billed** (the billing loop aborted early); tiers are now sorted and deduped before billing.
- **Custom class names**: every class is renameable (e.g. sewer classes), not just the c5–c7 slots.

## 2. Domain bugs found in review

- **USDA RD eligibility labels were inverted.** Step 8 prose correctly said grant eligibility requires the affordability index to *exceed* 1.5%, but the status labels on the same screen (and the PDF, Step 2 hints, and the AI prompt) said *"Below 1.5% — USDA RD eligible."* A board would read "grant eligible" exactly when the system is least in need. All surfaces now follow one convention: **burden above 1.5% of MHI supports the grant case**.
- **The 5-year "current rates" track subtracted *proposed* expenses.** `calc5Yr`'s current-budget parameter was dead code — every caller passed it, nothing used it. Current rates now pair with the current budget, proposed with proposed, and the charts/tables show both expense tracks.
- **Debt schedule & known items existed in the data model but did nothing.** `forecast.debtService[5]` and `knownItems[]` had no UI and fed no calculation. Step 5 now has editors for both: per-year debt service (replaces the budget's loan lines for that year — debt follows amortization, not inflation) and one-time items (positive = cost, negative = grant/revenue), applied to both tracks.
- **Five-Year Outlook mixed inflation bases**: expense rows hardcoded 3%/5% while the fund-balance row used the user's forecast rate — the rows couldn't reconcile. The fund balance now follows a "Projected Expenses (X% forecast)" row; 3%/5% remain as clearly labeled sensitivity rows.
- **Scenarios weren't persisted** — Step 6 kept them in local component state while the exporters read `study.activeScenario`, so PDFs always showed default multipliers. Scenarios now persist, and the affordability note reflects the residential multiplier instead of ignoring it.
- **Incomplete studies showed red zeros**: operating ratio 0.00 "Below break-even" when the budget simply wasn't entered yet. Metrics now return N/A with "insufficient data" states. A string MHI of `"0"` no longer reads as 0.00% "Affordable", and affordability keys off the *enabled* residential class.

## 3. New board-facing outputs (meeting items 4, 6–8)

- **True Cost of Service** (Step 4, Step 8, PDF, DOCX): annual operating expenses, annual gallons sold, true cost per 1,000 gal, average revenue per 1,000 gal, the gap, and the across-the-board adjustment needed to break even.
- **DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio)** — the covenant metric USDA RD / OWRB lenders actually require (≥ 1.10–1.25): added to the scorecard, report, exports, and AI benchmarks. (The existing consumer-style "Debt-to-Income < 45%" is retained but no longer the only debt metric.)
- **Data quality / liability statement** (meeting language) on the report screen and in every export, including which revenue basis the study used (distribution vs class averages). The expense section is unchanged, as requested.
- **Reserve target**: the arbitrary $5,000 default gets a one-click "3 months of O&M" suggestion.

## 4. Server-side AI for any Anthropic or OpenAI model (new)

`scripts/ai-proxy.js` — a **single dependency-free Node 18+ script** (same pattern as the existing geocode proxy):

```bash
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... AI_AUTH_TOKEN=code npm run ai-proxy
```

- Keys stay on the server. `GET /api/ai/config` advertises the enabled models; **staff pick the model in Step 7 → Settings** (Claude Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.1 / mini by default — all configurable via `ANTHROPIC_MODELS` / `OPENAI_MODELS`, and `OPENAI_BASE_URL` supports Azure/compatible endpoints).
- One provider-neutral endpoint: the app's existing Anthropic-shaped payload is translated to OpenAI Chat Completions automatically when an OpenAI model is chosen.
- Guardrails baked in: model allowlist, max_tokens cap, request-size cap, per-IP rate limiting, upstream timeout + retry, optional shared access code, logs that never contain prompt content.
- **One-container deploy**: the new `Dockerfile` builds the app against `/api/ai/messages` and serves app + AI from one port — `docker build -t wrstdy . && docker run -p 8788:8788 -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...` and you're done (no CORS).
- Client hardening: request timeouts, retry on 429/5xx, status-specific error messages, truncation notices, and empty responses now **throw** instead of silently saving a blank analysis with a fresh timestamp. Direct-browser mode (Anthropic-only) still works for local use and gains its own model picker.
- The Step 7 analyst prompt was updated: corrected USDA RD direction, DSCR + True Cost of Service benchmarks, usage-distribution awareness, and a closing data-quality reminder.

## 5. Smaller fixes

Map-import verification banner in Step 1 (meeting item 12 — e.g. the Tupelo supplier concern); import file-input reset on failure + newer-version warning; NaN lat/long can no longer reach Leaflet; switching studies no longer lands on the previous study's step; drafts advance to in-progress on any edit; PDF/DOCX render "chart unavailable" instead of silently dropping a failed chart; DOCX green/red delta conventions get legends.

## Testing

- `npm test`: **34 tests** — tier math (incl. 40k-gal overflow, unsorted tiers, sub-1k blocks), distribution revenue, the high-block acceptance case, DSCR, True Cost of Service, all `calc5Yr` tracks (current budget, debt schedule, known items, legacy compatibility), N/A metrics, and 12 proxy tests including a stubbed-upstream integration round trip. CI now runs tests before building.
- `npm run build` and `npm run build:single` both pass.
- End-to-end browser smoke (Chromium against the built app served by the proxy): all 8 steps render, the sample study's distribution drives revenue, the Step 7 model picker populates from the proxy config, **zero runtime errors**.

## Follow-ups (deliberately out of scope, per the meeting's priority order)

- CSV/Excel/AI import of billing reports (item 10) — the usage-distribution table is the landing zone for it.
- Asset Management Plan JSON import (item 11 — optional convenience).
- UI polish/animations (item 13 — after the team retests with Arkoma data).
- Suggested retest per item 14: load the Arkoma data, enter the usage distribution from the billing printouts, and confirm high-tier increases move monthly/annual revenue as expected.

items.title: fix(engine): respect explicit search depth in benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary
`getBestMoveDetailed` silently overrode any caller-supplied `maxDepth` with the Elo-derived depth whenever `timeParams.elo` was set. `engineMatch.ts` always sets `elo=2500`, so the `depth` field in `EngineMatchConfig` was dead — every match ran at the Elo-scaled depth 7. Benchmarks comparing "depth 8 vs 4" were actually measuring depth 7 vs depth 7, producing a false "depth is saturated" signal.

## Fix
- **js/aiEngine.ts**: explicit `timeParams.maxDepth` now overrides the Elo default (UI/worker callers pass no `maxDepth`, so unchanged behavior).
- **js/engineMatch.ts**: forward `engineConfig.depth` into `timeParams.maxDepth` so the override takes effect.
- **tools/benchmark.ts**: accept explicit depth args (7/8), report implied Elo diff from win-rate + engine stats (nps, blunders, maxDepth).
- **bench/*.txt**: documented baseline matches.

## Verification
- `npx tsc --noEmit` → 0 errors
- `npx vitest run tests/aiEngine.test.ts tests/search.invariant.test.ts tests/matchRefs.test.ts tests/aiEngine.eval.test.ts` → 37 passed
- Corrected benchmark (depth 3 vs depth 7, elo 2500, 24 games): **depth 7 beats depth 3 17:7 (+154 Elo)** — proving depth is NOT saturated once it is actually honored. (Earlier "19:18" e1200-vs-e2500 result was the bug: both sides ran at depth 7.)

## Risk
Minimal. Only `engineMatch` + benchmarking are affected; production UI/worker path is unchanged (no `maxDepth` passed → Elo scaling as before).

## Follow-up insight
The corrected depth-aware benchmark shows the engine still scales with depth, but self-play is ~78% draws (balanced vs balanced). Endgame/advantage conversion in the eval is the likely next lever, not more time.

items.title: feat(policy)!: migrate arg_patterns matching to RE2, eliminating ReDoS
items.body:
## Summary

A live-reproduced security gap: `Policy`'s `arg_patterns` regex matching used stdlib `re` (backtracking), matching policy-author-written patterns against attacker/agent-controlled content. A plausible, non-exotic pattern (`(\w+)+\d`) hung the process for **5+ seconds on a 31-byte payload** via catastrophic backtracking, with zero protection — reproduced live before any fix, and this was raised directly by the maintainer questioning whether the regex design scales.

Fix: migrate `arg_patterns` matching to [RE2](https://github.com/google/re2) (`google-re2`), which guarantees linear-time matching by construction — the same reason WAFs/IDS engines matching untrusted patterns against untrusted input use it. This eliminates the vulnerability class rather than mitigating a specific pattern shape. Verified live post-fix: the same pattern against a **200,000-byte** adversarial payload now resolves in **0.6ms**. Patterns are precompiled once per `Rule` (not once per `Policy.evaluate()` call), which is also the scaling fix, not just the safety one.

## Breaking changes

- RE2's syntax is a strict subset of Perl/PCRE — **no backreferences, no lookaround**. A pattern using either now fails to compile at policy-load time with a clear error. Verified: no shipped policy (example, bundled, or test) used either construct.
- Core package is **no longer zero-dependency** (`google-re2`).
- Python floor moves **3.9 → 3.10** (no `google-re2` wheel published for 3.9).

## Test plan
- [x] Exploit reproduced live pre-fix (5+ seconds, 31-byte payload); closed post-fix (0.6ms, 200,000-byte payload)
- [x] Mutation-tested: reverted to stdlib `re`, confirmed the new regression test hangs (exceeded even a 120s tool timeout on the same 200,000-byte payload)
- [x] New tests: ReDoS-closure bound, valid-pattern-still-matches, backreference/lookahead rejected at construction, RE2's C-level log noise confirmed suppressed
- [x] Full suite: `pytest -q` — 206 passed, 2 skipped
- [x] `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` clean (also fixed 5 pre-existing `typing.Callable` imports that the Python-floor bump newly flagged via ruff's target-version inference)

items.body:
Records the **async decision** (P2.1), replacing the "undecided" placeholder in `docs/performance.md` with a made decision + explicit trigger conditions.

## Verdict: defer the blanket async migration; tune and measure the synchronous path first
- `POST /api/chat` is a **sync** route → Starlette runs it in AnyIO's threadpool, so requests **already overlap** their network + DB waits. Sync is not serial.
- The **40 shared thread tokens** are *not* a guaranteed 40-request capacity — sync deps, file ops, background tasks, DB-pool/provider-connection limits, and CPU work all draw on the same pool.
- The existing **stub + in-memory** sweep removes the network/DB waiting that async targets, so it cannot settle the question; it emphasizes CPU-bound work async wouldn't help.

## Recommendation
Keep the sync API + stable 1.x contract. Instrument thread-token utilization, queueing, DB-pool checkout, provider latency, and stage CPU; **tune AnyIO tokens and the SQLAlchemy pool together**; use Uvicorn limits as overload protection (not capacity); move advisory conflict detection off the response-critical path; run the corrected benchmark against **Postgres + pgvector + a real LLM/embedding provider**. Reconsider async only when measured I/O-bound demand exceeds the tuned sync architecture — with enumerated trigger conditions and an incremental migration order if/when they're met.

Docs-only; no code change.

Completes the plan's Part 2 with what today actually established. The earlier update captured the first measurement; four corrections followed, and the corrections are the useful part.

## The benchmarks were lying in two different ways

Fixed and shipped in #7403. Discarding the result let Perry eliminate the loop; and even with it consumed, `fibonacci(FIB_N)` is loop-invariant, so it hoists out and runs **once** — checksum correct, `TOTAL` zero.

```ts
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000            // srem — fires
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000; a = a + 1 // frem — lost
```

Four wrong hypotheses about that subsystem are recorded so they aren't retried, along with why a careless widening is dangerous: it returns silently wrong integer arithmetic that `===` tests cannot see.

items.title: Fix train/val leakage, add held-out test eval, add regression tests
items.body:
## Why

The Phase 2 benchmark was measured on a leaking split, so its numbers were not trustworthy. Writing the final report or paper on top of them would have meant citing figures that later had to be retracted.

## Leakage

`build_wheel_dataset.py` shuffled `(image_path, bbox)` pairs at **crop** level and sliced by index, so several vehicles from the same COCO photo landed on both sides of the split — sharing scene, lighting, camera, resolution.

| Class | Leak-prone crops |
|---|---|
| 2-wheeler | 76% |
| 4-wheeler | **91%** |
| 6+ wheeler | 65% |

A second defect: the 3-wheeler class used **whole photos** while every other class used tight crops.

Both fixed — split by source image, and the auto-rickshaw arm now crops from its YOLO labels.

## Corrected benchmark

| Model | Was (leaky) | Now (clean) |
|---|---|---|
| SmallCNN | 0.751 | **0.787** |
| RTMDet-CSPNeXt | 0.683 | **0.695** |
| YOLOv8-cls *(selected)* | 0.867 | **0.861** |

Ranking is unchanged, so the model-selection conclusion is robust. Because both defects changed at once, the deltas are **not** attributable to leakage alone — the report states this.

**A hypothesis I had was disproved:** I suspected 3-wheeler's 0.96 F1 came from the whole-photo shortcut. After cropping it still scores 0.96 — auto-rickshaws are simply distinctive. What actually fell was 4-wheeler (0.81 → 0.70) and 6+ wheeler (0.78 → 0.72); 4-wheeler was the most leak-prone class at 91%, which is the pattern leakage predicts.

## First clean helmet number

mAP@50 **0.764** on the 52-image held-out test split, never previously touched. (0.731 val was used for epoch selection, so it was optimistically biased.) Test > val is small-split variance, not a better model — both corroborate at ~0.73–0.76.

Passenger-helmet classes are weakest on **both** splits (0.545 / 0.565), confirming issue #8 is a real data limitation rather than a split artifact.

## Tests

Adds `tests/` covering every defect that has actually shipped here: inverted compliance, config/weights mismatch, split leakage, and silent DeepSORT/OSNet fallbacks — plus CI. The leakage guard is mutation-tested (fails on an injected leak, passes when clean).

All 7 tests pass.

Runs the same deep out-of-sample test x53 ran on Gap Widen, now on the Z-Score book's own MIO universe.

## Pre-registered gates (fixed before computing)

1. Executable CAGR > 0 at the 0.05%/side standard.
2. Executable CAGR > equal-weight buy-and-hold of the **same names**, 2011–2018.

Gate 1 passes. Gate 2 fails.

## Result

| Era | Names | Book CAGR | DD | PF | Buy & hold | B&H DD | Excess |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deep 2011–2018 | 313 | 10.08% | −28.0% | 1.42 | 11.65% | −22.7% | **−1.57pp** |
| Recent 2019–2026 (same names) | 313 | 53.75% | −18.4% | 2.69 | 17.73% | −42.3% | **+36.02pp** |

Book column is executable basis (MOO entry + 3:45 MOC exit, mean of 5 perturbation seeds). Idealized deep CAGR 13.85%, PF 1.53, 683 trades.

## Reading it honestly

- **Not Gap Widen's failure.** Gap Widen went to ~zero in the deep era and lost to its universe by ~10pp at double the drawdown. Z-Score stays clearly profitable and merely stops *adding* anything over owning the same names.
- **Indistinguishable from zero, not negative.** Seeds run 6.22 / 9.53 / 9.94 / 11.27 / 13.44 — two of five beat the 11.65% hurdle. A −1.57pp mean sits inside that spread.
- **Verdict recorded: era-dependent.** Every book in this program tested across eras has now failed at least one. Book stays on paper; the 20-closed-forward-trade real-money gate is unchanged.

## Correction shipped with the result

The first pass reported **PASS by 0.77pp** on 325 names. It was contaminated: Robinhood returned `interpolated: true` synthetic bars for 24 deep-window symbols (several ~95% synthetic — BE real only from 2018-07-25, BILI from 2018-03-28). These are zero-volume flat-price rows, the same padding defect x45 found. Unlike the in-session `gw_harness`, the lab's `fillmode_sim` does **not** filter zero-volume rows, so they entered the simulation. Rebuilding the store (drop `volume<=0`, require ≥300 real bars) dropped 12 names, truncated 77 series, and flipped the verdict PASS → FAIL. Only the clean run is reported; the contaminated run is disclosed on the card.

## Changes

- `data/x54_zscore_deep.json` — full record, both legs, all seeds.
- `docs/x54_results_zscore_deep_oos.md` — gates, result, correction, caveats.
- `index.html`:
  - new x54 card with the correction and survivorship caveat behind a details toggle
  - "Deep era 2011-18 (x54)" tile on the Z-Score card
  - Today tab tier for ZSCORE moved to REGIME-DEP with the reasoning
  - Z-Score `status` string records the era finding
  - benchmark-gate note corrected — it claimed Gap Widen RSI2 was the only book to fail that test in any era, which x53 and x54 both supersede

## Verification

All 15 blobs parse, `node --check` clean on the extracted script, Playwright smoke suite **34/34** with no page errors (5 new checks guard the x54 card, tile, verdict, contamination disclosure, and the corrected benchmark note).

## Caveats

Survivorship — the deep universe is today's survivors, which biases both the book and its hurdle up, which is why they are compared to each other rather than an absolute bar. 45 of the 358 live MIO names have no 2011–2018 history and are absent from both sides. Deep-era bars are Robinhood-sourced; the recent row is the audited Tradier basis.

items.title: test(overlayfs): add single-layer hot-reload perf benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #235.

Benchmark-only change for detecting hot-reload regressions when sync strategies change one layer. Scope settled on:
- OverlayFS single-layer reload: warm neg-cache, `ReplaceLayer(content, newFS)`, then resolve the changed path.
- OverlayFS targeted invalidation vs full invalidation baseline with the same warm-cache cycle and post-invalidation resolves, so spared neg-cache entries make the single-layer benefit observable.
- Content rescan/re-index benchmark using the clean `content.Scanner.Scan` entry point called by `cmd/blogflow`'s reloader.

No production code changes; CHANGELOG skipped.

## Reload path found

Sync strategies (`watch`, `webhook`, `sidecar`, `poll`) call `gitops.ContentReloader`. In `cmd/blogflow/reload.go`, that reloads config, reloads theme templates, runs `scanner.Scan(fsys)`, swaps the handler index, then flushes the render cache. Overlay layer swaps are supported by `OverlayFS.ReplaceLayer`, which atomically replaces one layer and invalidates affected negative-cache entries.

## Benchmark numbers

Command:

```sh
go test -run '^$' -bench 'ReplaceLayer|InvalidateLayer|InvalidateAll|ContentReindex' -benchtime=100ms ./internal/overlayfs/ ./internal/content/
```

Results on darwin/amd64, VirtualApple @ 2.50GHz:

```text
BenchmarkReplaceLayer_SingleLayer-16        255     488132 ns/op       768 B/op       7 allocs/op
BenchmarkInvalidateLayer_SingleLayer-16       1  111747667 ns/op   5530464 B/op   37897 allocs/op
BenchmarkInvalidateAll_WarmNegCache-16        1  163479376 ns/op   7261152 B/op   59673 allocs/op
BenchmarkContentReindex-16                    7   15514470 ns/op  13283083 B/op   92104 allocs/op
```

`InvalidateLayer_SingleLayer` is meaningfully cheaper than `InvalidateAll_WarmNegCache` because the fixture now warms mostly content-layer entries that survive a config-layer invalidation; the full wipe has to rebuild those entries during the timed post-invalidation resolve phase.

## Validation

- `go build ./...` ✅
- `go vet ./...` ✅
- `golangci-lint run ./internal/overlayfs/... ./internal/content/...` ✅
- `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/overlayfs/... ./internal/content/...` ✅
- Corrected benchmarks command above ✅

items.title: fix(benchmark): corrected_rate_hz was 42% high whenever min_confidence was set
items.body:
## The bug

`corrected_rate_hz` was `fidelity.rate_hz * purity / efficiency`. Those quantities sit on **opposite sides of a post-decode filter**:

- `rate_hz` is the HMM's `p_flip`, estimated **before** `min_confidence` drops anything
- `efficiency` / `purity` are measured on surrogates reconstructed **with** the filter applied

So the correction overstates the rate by exactly the fraction the cut removes. On the reference device at `min_confidence=0.4`:

| seed | true | before | err | after | err |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 57.2 | 81.4 | +42% | 55.2 | −3% |
| 1 | 67.2 | 93.8 | +40% | 65.8 | −2% |
| 2 | 71.8 | 102.5 | +43% | 73.5 | +2% |
| 3 | 57.6 | 87.6 | +52% | 62.3 | +8% |
| 4 | 60.6 | 84.7 | +40% | 59.3 | −2% |
| 5 | 69.0 | 93.3 | +35% | 66.4 | −4% |

**mean |error|: 42% → 4%**

Found because the reported count and the reported rate disagreed on the same trace: 214 flips over 5 s is 42.8 Hz, while `rate_hz` read 61.0 Hz.

## The fix

Invert the bias on the count the pipeline **actually output** — `n_flips / duration` — which is the quantity the surrogate-measured efficiency and purity describe. The identity `n_pred * purity / efficiency == n_truth` only holds when the count and the rates refer to the same flip list.

With no cut the two forms agree (60.6 vs 61.0 Hz on the reference trace), so **nothing changes for anyone not using `min_confidence`** — verified at 2.1% mean absolute error, statistically indistinguishable from before.

Also switches to the pooled efficiency/purity rather than mean-of-ratios, since this is an inversion of ratios of totals.

## What deliberately did not change

`rate_hz` stays **pre-cut**. It is what the surrogates are *injected* at, and there you want the process rate, not the post-filter count — injecting 42.8 Hz when the device runs at 67 Hz would make every surrogate too easy. That asymmetry is now stated in both docstrings and §12c.

It also remains the "measured" marker in `plot_efficiency_vs_rate`, which is correct for the same reason: it is the best available estimate of where the device sits on the rate axis.

## Verification

**98 checks, all passing** (was 94). New ones: `corrected_rate_hz` recovers the true rate to better than 15% at both `min_confidence=0.0` and `0.4`; the cut reduces the reported count (303 → 214); and it leaves `rate_hz` untouched (61.00 vs 61.00 Hz).

55-check regression gate still passes.

items.title: Corrected filter-effectiveness benchmark + negative-selection study
items.body:
## What
A corrected negative-sampling benchmark that overturns the old "filters are worse than random" headline, plus a full negative-selection study (Tiers 1–3 + PSM + eval-match). All numbers are committed 3-seed runs; see `docs/FILTER-EFFECTIVENESS.md`.

## Headline results
- The old **−0.097** deficit was a **benchmark artifact** (6k-positive cap → isolation shortcut, unequal pools, 100% hard-tail selection). Fixed: one frozen veto-cleaned pool, un-capped positives, degree-stratified reporting.
- At proper coverage the full stack (**`stacked`**) **beats random** on AUROC/AUPRC and is the **purest** arm; `topology_hard` (old default) is the only consistent loser. Model-robust (RF + LightGBM), dataset-robust (HuRI + DRYAD).
- **Injection backtest**: `topology_hard` selects **~75%** of injected hidden positives; `stacked`/`safe` catch ~100%. The damage holds under both learners (LGBM is *more* hurt).

## Product change
- `PipelineConfig.train_selection` (`matching.py::select_train`) — `hard | safe | stacked | mixture`, **default `stacked`** (the pipeline no longer emits only the losing hard tail).
- Fusion docstring marked as uncalibrated heuristic; `KnownPositiveVeto.certification()` (fail-closed).

## Negative-selection study (in the doc, §5)
- **Mixture** — doesn't beat `stacked` (unverified hard = contaminated dead weight).
- **Counterfactual** — loses (matching to positives re-contaminates, ~50% hidden positives).
- **PSM** — clean-pool matching fixes ~60% of the counterfactual's deficit but still trails (distribution mismatch).
- **eval-match** — matching to the held-out **evaluation** population (not positives) beats random in every cell and ties/beats `stacked` in 2/4. Converging lesson: **clean + representative-of-the-evaluation is the right objective, never matched-to-positives.**

items.title: Perf(optim-proofs): bisection iters 80→53 + FFI wrapper + corrected benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary

- Reduce `projectL1F`/`bisectThetaF` bisection iterations from 80 to 53 (IEEE 754 mantissa precision ceiling), eliminating 37.5% of inner-loop work. Measured ~1.5x speedup across all scenarios.
- Add `portfolio-proofs/lean_pgd_ffi.py`: Cython FFI wrapper with condition-number-based dispatch (FFI-flat for cond<150, FFI-boxed for cond≥150).
- Correct the misleading "~3ms" performance comment in `PGDFlat.lean` — actual warm latency is 2–233ms depending on problem structure.
- Correct benchmark JSON with measured timings (iters=53, warm subprocess, Apple M-series).
- Fix CLAUDE.md typo: "Six failure scenarios" → "Seven failure scenarios".

## Bisection precision analysis

IEEE 754 `Float` has a 53-bit mantissa. After `k` bisection steps the range shrinks by 2^(-k):
- **Inner bisect** (theta s.t. Σ softThresh(yᵢ - θ, μ) = B): range ≈ 8; need precision ≤ tol_pgd/N ≈ 1e-9; k ≥ 33.
- **Outer bisect** (μ ≥ 0 s.t. leverage = L, tol 1e-11): range ≈ 4; need 4/2^k × N < 1e-11; k ≥ 43.

`iters=53` satisfies both with a ~10-step safety margin and equals the machine-precision ceiling.

## Corrected timing table (warm subprocess, iters=53)

| Problem | Before | After | Speedup | CV% |
|---------|--------|-------|---------|-----|
| N=2 diag (pipe floor) | 2.4ms | 2.0ms | 1.2x | 3.0% |
| N=5 diag phantom_pos | 4.8ms | 3.5ms | 1.4x | 1.1% |
| N=3 diag vix_shock | 7.6ms | 6.4ms | 1.2x | 1.3% |
| N=10 CAPM cond=36 | 83ms | 56ms | 1.5x | 0.9% |
| N=10 rand cond=204 | 344ms | 233ms | 1.5x | 0.4% |

## FFI path finding

The Cython FFI path (subprocess replaced by in-process call) provides **no benefit** for FFI-flat: same Lean code, same `FloatArray.get!` bounds checks, same compute time. Pipe adds only ~0.3ms. items.title: perf: O(1) select-by-ID in DBSQLMemoryAdapter; add JSON and DB benchmarks
items.body:
Adds JSON and DB benchmark suites, and one optimization they turned up.

## The optimization: O(1) select-by-ID in `DBSQLMemoryAdapter`

`_selectEntries` answered *every* condition by scanning the table `Map` and evaluating the condition per row — including a `ConditionID`, even though that `Map` is keyed by ID and the adapter already has an O(1) lookup helper. So `selectByID` was O(rows):

| rows | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 7.80 µs | 7.13 µs |
| 50 | 9.73 µs | 7.16 µs |
| 400 | 25.26 µs | **7.22 µs** |

Now flat. A lookup miss falls through to the original scan, so a `ConditionID` whose value doesn't match a key exactly (a `String` `'7'` against an `int` `7`) resolves exactly as before — just as slowly as it always did. Results are unchanged either way.

This mostly speeds up the test suite and development, since the memory adapter is where those run.

## A correction

An earlier commit on this branch claimed the cost of a query "is the repository/transaction machinery". **That was wrong**, and I'd published it before checking. Scaling the row count shows `selectByQuery` is linear:

| rows | `selectByQuery` |
|---|---|
| 10 | 10.9 µs |
| 50 | 20.4 µs |
| 400 | 105.9 µs |

≈ 8.5 µs fixed + ~0.24 µs/row. The number was dominated by the memory adapter's scan, which a real SQL adapter never pays. Only the fixed part is shared framework cost. `benchmark/README.md`, the CHANGELOG and the in-file comments now say so, and the DB suite takes `--rows=N` so the two can be separated.

## What the suites show otherwise

**JSON needs nothing.** `Json.encodeToSink` — the response path — runs close to a bare `dart:convert` encode (~1.5 µs vs ~1.2 µs, small map) and is *faster* on larger payloads, since it writes bytes to a sink instead of building a `String`. Request bodies go through `dart:convert` directly, so there's no layer to remove.

**DB**, at 50 rows:

| | µs/op |
|---|---|
| `ConditionParseCache.parseQuery` (cached) | 0.010 |
| `Entity.toJson` | 0.074 |
| `generateSelectSQL` | 0.83 |
| `EntityHandler.createFromMap` | 1.12 |
| `ConditionParser.parse` (shared parser) | 2.74 |
| `Transaction.executeBlock` (**empty**) | 2.43 |
| `repository.selectByID` | 7.26 |

The two things a query is assumed to be expensive for are not: parsing is cached at ~300× cheaper than parsing, and SQL generation is under a microsecond.

## Two hypotheses that failed

Recorded so they aren't re-tried:

1. **Per-response `JsonEncoder`.** `Json._buildJsonEncoder` returns the cached `defaultEncoder` only when *every* argument is defaulted — and the response path always passes `toEncodable`, so it builds a fresh encoder each time. Memoizing it (safe: `autoResetEntityCache` defaults to `true`) moved the small-map encode **1.555 → 1.522 µs** and made the 50-map case slightly *worse*. Noise.
2. **Eager `Completer`s.** `Transaction` creates three in its constructor despite the fields being `late final`. Making them lazy left an empty `executeBlock` at **2.40 µs**, unchanged.

Neither is included.

## Another measurement error worth flagging

My first DB run reported `ConditionParser.parse` at **125 µs**, which looked like a major find. It was my benchmark constructing a `ConditionParser` per iteration — the cost is PetitParser building the grammar lazily. `bones_api` holds it in a `static final`, so it's a one-off startup cost and there's no bug. The corrected benchmark reuses the parser (2.74 µs), with a note in the README since a per-query parser *would* be catastrophic.

## Where to look next

`Transaction.executeBlock` — 2.4 µs for an *empty* block is the floor under every DB operation and the largest remaining fixed cost. That wants a real profiler (`dart run --observe`), not more micro-benchmarks.

The DB suite carries a small self-contained `BenchUser` entity so it doesn't depend on the test fixtures.

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `dart test --exclude-tags docker` | 783 passed |
| `dart analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings .` | clean |
| `dart format -o none --set-exit-if-changed .` | clean |
